name: Daily Mail cryptic crossword, book 2 No 50

book.title: Daily Mail New Cryptic Crosswords, volume 2

clue.text: She might be suffering from a bad line

indicators.note: something suffering is damaged and out of shape, so the letters beside it are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A woman on a crackling telephone connection is having a hard time hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' stands for any woman's name, here BELINDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Belinda is a female first name, so a woman could be referred to as she.

clue.text: His tribe could shortly become like people here

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the last letter of the word before is dropped
letters that become something else are rearranged into it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, before being cut short

explanation.surface: A man's clan might soon turn into something resembling the locals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People here' assumes the solver is in Britain, where the clue was published.
explanation.definitionFit: British describes the inhabitants of Britain, the nationality of the newspaper's own readers.

clue.text: Like obsessive museum visitors who can't keep up?

definitions.text: Like obsessive museum visitors who can't keep up?

blocks.note: surface reading: people who spend all their time among historical exhibits
setter's reading: people who are out of date and refuse to accept modern ways

explanation.surface: Devoted museum-goers who never move with the times.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase describes old-fashioned people, and also, literally, anyone who seems to live among relics.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stuck in old attitudes and unable to adapt to the present is said to dwell in bygone days.

clue.text: Nothing short of a great river

indicators.note: something falling short lacks its end, so the final letter is removed

blocks.note: the Nile, the great river of Africa

explanation.surface: A modest boast that a flow almost matches a mighty river.
explanation.definitionFit: Nil is zero, especially as a sports score, meaning nothing at all.

clue.text: Don't start to praise the item you check

indicators.note: not starting means the first letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: to laud is to praise
it as a pronoun stands for the thing

explanation.surface: Advice not to begin admiring the thing you are inspecting.
explanation.walkthrough: LAUD loses its first letter to leave AUD.
explanation.definitionFit: To audit accounts is to examine and verify them officially, an inspection or check.

clue.text: What's wrong with the old woman meeting someone respectable?

blocks.note: an informal word for one's mother
a well-bred, respectable woman

explanation.surface: Someone asks what upsets an elderly woman about being introduced to a proper, respectable person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting' only puts the two pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A malady is an illness or ailment, the thing that is wrong with a patient.

clue.text: One doesn't need a blow to go over the water

definitions.text: One doesn't need a blow to go over the water

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who need not be struck

blocks.clueFragment: a blow to go over the water
blocks.note: setter's reading: a blow is a wind, and an engine-driven vessel needs no wind to cross water

explanation.surface: Someone crossing water without needing to be hit.
explanation.walkthrough: A blow is a strong wind; unlike a sailing boat, this craft has an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorboat is a vessel powered by an engine, so it can travel without wind in sails.

clue.text: With a bit of luck cardinal could be attracted

blocks.note: the first two letters of luck, a small part of the word
cardinal red is a deep scarlet colour, named after cardinals' robes

explanation.surface: With some good fortune, a senior churchman might be won over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' suggests the churchman, but here it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lured means enticed or tempted, drawn in as if by bait.

clue.text: Make a lot of money selling lions?

blocks.note: the setter's meaning: business is booming
the pun: lions roar, so trade in them would be literally roaring

explanation.surface: A dealer gets rich from a trade in big cats.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for thriving business is taken literally for animals that roar.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a business that is selling briskly and earning plenty of profit.

clue.text: Reward by not going round to take a turn

indicators.note: a turn swings something round, so the word to is read backwards
going round something encloses it, so one piece wraps around the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
un is the prefix meaning not

explanation.surface: A prize is earned by staying put rather than taking your turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' looks like a plain negative, but it supplies the prefix meaning not; the reversed little word holds it, and the whole sits inside the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A bounty is a sum offered as a prize, for example for capturing a criminal.

clue.text: Being disabled maybe having no effect

blocks.note: first meaning, stressed on the first syllable: a person weakened by illness or disability
second meaning, stressed on the second syllable: void, not valid

explanation.surface: A remark that a disability may leave someone without influence.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are pronounced differently: IN-valid and in-VAL-id.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a sick or disabled person; the adjective describes a ticket or law that is void and carries no force.

clue.text: Rent fuss causing a storm

blocks.note: rent as the past participle of rend: ripped
ado is bother or fuss

explanation.surface: A row over rent money provokes a furious argument between landlord and tenant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid for housing, but it is the old verb meaning torn.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent rotating windstorm, a particularly destructive kind of storm.

clue.text: Accepted name for somewhere to stay

blocks.note: in means fashionable or accepted
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A recognised name is wanted for a place to lodge.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn is a pub offering lodging, a place travellers spend the night.

clue.text: Modified view of feathers in the rain?

blocks.note: first meaning: made weaker or less extreme
second, punning meaning: soft plumage that has been soaked by rain

explanation.surface: A softened opinion is pictured as a bird's plumage getting soaked in a shower.
explanation.walkthrough: Down is the fine soft feathering of birds, so feathers out in the rain are literally watered down.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion that has been weakened or toned down is described as diluted, like a drink with water added.

clue.text: See if you have the time

blocks.note: first meaning: look at or observe
second meaning: a timepiece worn on the wrist, which you check if you have the time

explanation.surface: An invitation to come and look if you can spare a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If you have the time' reads as politeness, but it describes the wrist-worn device.
explanation.definitionFit: To watch is to look at attentively; a watch is also a small timepiece worn on the wrist.

clue.text: Lift one among many

indicators.note: a thing placed among others sits in their midst, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a host is a great number, as in a host of reasons
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: One person in a crowd gets raised up.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoist is to raise something up, especially with ropes or a crane, which is a synonym of lift.

clue.text: Too bold to deceive a writer

blocks.note: to fool someone is to trick them
Thomas Hardy, the English novelist and poet

explanation.surface: Trying to trick an author is a rash undertaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolhardy means recklessly daring, brave beyond the point of sense.

clue.text: No staff man is at liberty to take much from a knight

indicators.note: taking much of a word keeps most of it, so its tail is cut off

blocks.note: at liberty means free
Sir Lancelot, knight of King Arthur's Round Table

explanation.surface: A man without employees can help himself to a knight's possessions.
explanation.walkthrough: Much of LANCELOT is LANCE. 'No staff man' means someone not on the payroll.
explanation.definitionFit: A freelance is self-employed and works for various clients, so is not on any firm's permanent payroll.

clue.text: Not yielding with nothing in store

indicators.note: with something in it means holding it inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: hard means firm and unyielding
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to give way when the cupboard is bare.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard is a hidden stockpile of valuables or supplies, a stock kept in reserve.

clue.text: Mad chemist is missing, unable to go around collecting water

indicators.note: the word is goes missing, so those two letters are dropped from the word before
mad suggests disorder, so the remaining letters are jumbled
going around something means enclosing it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: can't, without its apostrophe, means unable to
taken as written, before the deletion

explanation.surface: A crazed scientist has vanished, too helpless to wander about, while gathering water samples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad chemist' looks like one phrase, but the chemist first loses 'is', then the leftovers are jumbled and wrapped in the contraction for unable.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchment is an area of land that gathers rainfall and drains it into a river or reservoir.

clue.text: Convention requires copper to be most adaptable

indicators.note: something adaptable can be changed in form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: Tradition demands that a police officer be as flexible as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a police officer, but here it is the chemical element.
explanation.definitionFit: A custom is an established practice or tradition, a social convention.

clue.text: Cancel article left out of book

indicators.note: something left out of a whole is omitted from it, so letters are removed

blocks.note: an annual is a book published once a year, often for children
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An item has been omitted from a publication and so must be scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: One A is dropped from ANNUAL, leaving ANNUL.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul a marriage or contract is to declare it void, which formally cancels it.

clue.text: They may give lifts when snakes are avoided

definitions.text: They may give lifts when snakes are avoided

blocks.note: surface reading: drivers offering rides
setter's reading: a children's board game in which snakes send a counter down and other squares carry it up

explanation.surface: Kindly motorists offer rides once dangerous reptiles have been dodged.
explanation.walkthrough: In Snakes and Ladders, snakes send a counter down and the other pieces of equipment carry it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladders raise climbers upward, and in the children's board game they move counters up the board.

clue.text: Side place is possibly adapted to conditions

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters before could be arranged in another way

blocks.note: the three words used as letters

explanation.surface: A location off to one side may suit particular circumstances.
explanation.definitionFit: An organism or tool that is specialised has evolved or been designed for a particular environment or task.

clue.text: It shows who one is on an island in a manner of speaking

blocks.note: ID is identification, a card proving identity
IOM is the abbreviation for the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A statement that one's identity is shown on an island, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just joins the ID to the island abbreviation that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is an expression peculiar to a language, a characteristic way of phrasing things.

clue.text: Being a good chap, the military man giving orders isn't complaining

blocks.note: surface reading: being a decent fellow

blocks.clueFragment: the military man giving orders isn't complaining
blocks.note: setter's reading: someone who accepts orders without grumbling is called a good one of these

explanation.surface: A soldier in charge is a decent fellow who doesn't grumble.
explanation.walkthrough: A good sport is a man who takes things cheerfully and without complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A sport is a fair-minded, generous person who accepts setbacks cheerfully, as in being a good sport.

clue.text: He would find debts boring

blocks.note: surface reading: a man for whom money owed is dull
setter's reading: debts are IOUS, and adding them to this man's name gives a word for boring

explanation.surface: A man who finds his unpaid bills tedious to deal with.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: the answer is a man's name which, followed by IOUS (debts), makes TEDIOUS, meaning boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Ted is a common short form of Edward, a man's name, so he can stand for him.

clue.text: Something new leaving the pub to show approval

definitions.note: the answer is a noun: a show of approval

indicators.note: one thing leaving another departs from it, so its letters are taken away

blocks.note: an innovation is a new idea or device
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A newcomer walks out of the bar to applause.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing INN from the front of INNOVATION leaves OVATION.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovation is sustained applause from an audience, a public demonstration of approval.

clue.text: Fury at being given the sack?

definitions.text: Fury at being given the sack

blocks.note: someone sacked from a job is out
rage is violent anger

explanation.surface: A worker is livid on being fired.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the rage of someone thrown out of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrage is intense indignation or anger, a strong response to injustice such as an unfair dismissal.

clue.text: Can this be money?

blocks.note: first meaning: a metal container for food
second meaning: old British slang for cash

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether something could really be worth cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb, but it is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin is a sealed metal food container, and in dated British slang the word also meant cash.

clue.text: Ties my knot in a difficult situation

indicators.note: tying a knot twists things together, so the letters before are tangled into a new order

blocks.note: the two words used as letters

explanation.surface: Someone complains that their tie has become tangled in a tricky moment.
explanation.walkthrough: A stymie was originally a golf position in which an opponent's ball blocks the line to the hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A stymie is an obstruction or predicament, a situation that blocks progress.

clue.text: Gives one of the trees away

blocks.note: first meaning: offers formally, as in tendering payment
the second half's wordplay is unclear as printed

explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'Gives' is clear, but the rest of the clue as printed does not yield a convincing wordplay; it may be garbled in the book's text.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender is to offer or present something formally, such as money or a resignation.
